messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Bao, a 24-year-old painter, sits rigidly in his chair, his hands clenched in his lap. He speaks of the last six months as if describing a foreign country he has unwillingly come to inhabit. The trauma occurred in the place that was once his sanctuary: the small, light-filled studio attached to his apartment. His then-partner, Kenji, had locked him in after a minor argument escalated. Bao remembers the sound of the deadbolt clicking, the sudden shift in Kenji’s eyes, and the terrifying uncertainty of what would come next. The ensuing physical assault is a blur of disjointed sensory snapshots. He has a crystal-clear memory of the smell of turpentine and the precise pattern of the wood grain on the floorboards where he was pinned, but he cannot recall how the argument ended or how he got out of the room. This confusing sequence of events haunts him, a film reel with crucial frames missing.

These fragmented memories are not passive recollections; they are active ambushes. An unwanted thought of Kenji’s voice (a trigger) can instantly plunge him back into the studio, the memory so vivid he can feel the cold floor against his cheek, as if it is happening right now. This reliving of the event (Memory) immediately activates his sense of profound danger (Threat). His heart will pound, and he will begin scanning the room for exits, even in his own familiar living space. The intense fear sparked by the memory reinforces his core belief that he is inadequate, a person who was too weak to prevent what happened. This deep-seated sense of personal failing (Negative Appraisals) is a constant undercurrent, whispering that the event occurred because of the sort of person he is.

His life has become a complex map of avoidance and hypervigilance, governed by a pervasive sense of threat. The belief that he is fundamentally unsafe (Negative Appraisals) means he is constantly on high alert. This state of threat monitoring, in turn, generates its own triggers; he finds himself listening for the faint sound of footsteps outside his door or the jingle of keys, each noise a potential prelude to intrusion. Any unexpected delay—his current partner running ten minutes late from the grocery store—becomes proof that something terrible is happening. This feeling of imminent danger (Threat) often forces him into a state of paralysis; when he hears a sudden noise at night, he will freeze completely in his bed, a reaction that only deepens his self-appraisal as helpless and inadequate. These moments of freezing (Maladaptive Strategy) do nothing to resolve the threat, instead leaving him trapped with his thoughts, which inevitably drift back to fragmented images of the assault (Memory).

The feedback loops are now tightly woven into the fabric of his days. A trigger, such as feeling watched while sketching in a public park, will not only activate his threat system but also his impulse to flee or shut down. He has stopped going to parks entirely. This avoidance of situations that might bring on the feelings of being trapped (Maladaptive Strategies) has shrunk his world, reinforcing his belief that he no longer belongs anywhere. At night, he puts off going to sleep, terrified of the nightmares, a strategy that leaves him exhausted and only makes the intrusive memories more potent the next day. The very act of avoiding anything that reminds him of Kenji—a particular musician, a brand of tea, the colour green—serves as a constant reminder of the trauma, bringing forth unwanted thoughts (Triggers) and confirming his own sense of being permanently broken (Negative Appraisals).

Bao sought therapy after an incident last week. His new partner, meaning only to be affectionate, came up behind him while he was painting and placed his hands on his shoulders. Bao froze instantly, dropping his brush. The terror in his eyes was unmistakable, and the ensuing silence was filled with a shame so profound he could barely speak. He realized then that his internal world of threat was beginning to poison the first safe relationship he had known since the assault. He came to therapy not just to escape the memories, but because of a desperate fear that if he cannot change, he will lose the very connection that makes him feel he might one day belong somewhere again.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not demonstrate how the patient's negative beliefs cause him to develop or perceive new triggers.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not demonstrate how the trauma memory itself causes new things to become triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette does not demonstrate how a general feeling of threat causes the trauma memory to surface.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The vignette does not demonstrate how the patient's maladaptive strategies (e.g., avoidance) lead to an increased sense of threat.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
An unwanted thought of Kenji’s voice (a trigger) can instantly plunge him back into the studio, the memory so vivid he can feel the cold floor against his cheek, as if it is happening right now.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Because the memory intrudes with such sensory force, elements from it have begun to contaminate his present; he now finds the smell of turpentine or the sight of dark wood flooring can unexpectedly trigger the same wave of panic.
<<<END>>>
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The belief that he is fundamentally unsafe means he is constantly on high alert.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Because he is so convinced that danger is everywhere and that he is incapable of handling it, ordinary sounds he once would have ignored now snag his attention as potential threats.
<<<END>>>
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Any unexpected delay—his current partner running ten minutes late from the grocery store—becomes proof that something terrible is happening.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
This persistent sense of danger keeps his mind close to the event, as if needing to review it to stay one step ahead of a similar attack, which makes it far more likely that fragmented images of the assault will surface.
<<<END>>>
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He has stopped going to parks entirely.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
By never testing his fear, he has inadvertently confirmed it; his nervous system interprets the successful avoidance as proof that the park was, in fact, dangerous, leaving his underlying sense of threat not only intact but strengthened.
<<<END>>>
